title: Route AI Agents Across Models with NVIDIA NeMo Switchyard | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: NVIDIA has open-sourced NeMo Switchyard, a provider-agnostic model-routing layer that sends each step of an agent workload to the model best suited to it rather than defaulting to the largest frontier model. The headline evidence: LangChain measured a 74% cost reduction on a 145-task agentic suite by routing only 7% of calls to Claude Opus 4.8 (the rest to NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning) for a ~6-point accuracy loss, while Cognition's Devin Desktop hit 50.6% on FrontierCode Main at ~28% lower mean cost, within 2.8 points of Opus 5. The strategic subtext is that NVIDIA is standardizing the layer that decides how much traffic frontier closed-model APIs get.

insights.claim: LangChain benchmarked NVIDIA NeMo Switchyard's escalation router across 145 multi-turn agentic tasks and measured a 74% cost reduction versus a frontier-only baseline while sending just 7% of calls to the frontier model, at roughly a 6-point accuracy tradeoff.
insights.speaker: Tanay Varshney
insights.so_what: If 93% of agent calls can leave the frontier tier for a 6-point accuracy hit, per-token revenue projections for closed frontier APIs in agentic workloads are exposed to a step-function repricing.
insights.quote: delivered a 74% cost reduction compared with a frontier-only baseline across five runs, sending just 7% of calls to the frontier model, at a measured ~6-point accuracy tradeoff
insights.locator: LangChain benchmarked NeMo Switchyard using its internal

insights.claim: Cognition deployed NeMo Switchyard staged routing in Devin Desktop and on the FrontierCode Main benchmark scored 50.6% at a $3.11 mean cost by routing between Opus 5 and Kimi K2.7 — within 2.8 percentage points of Opus 5 accuracy at approximately 28% lower mean cost.
insights.speaker: Tanay Varshney
insights.so_what: A production coding agent proving near-frontier quality at ~28% lower cost sets the new bar for agent unit economics and pressures anyone selling frontier-only agent seats.
insights.quote: achieving 50.6% at a $3.11 mean cost—within 2.8 percentage points of Opus 5 accuracy at approximately 28% lower mean cost

insights.claim: Sending every request to the largest available model raises both cost and latency, while defaulting to a small model degrades quality on complex tasks — making the single-model agent architecture strictly dominated on mixed workloads.
insights.speaker: Tanay Varshney
insights.so_what: The framing that kills the 'pick one model' procurement decision; enterprise AI spend shifts toward multi-vendor pools plus an arbitration layer.
insights.quote: Sending every request to the largest model can increase cost and latency, while sending every request to a smaller model can reduce quality on complex tasks.
insights.locator: Building an AI agent does not end with choosing

insights.claim: The routing objective is explicitly not to identify the strongest model but to select the model most likely to meet a required quality level at the right cost, with each candidate scored on a blend of predicted accuracy, cost, and latency.
insights.speaker: Tanay Varshney
insights.so_what: Reframes model competition from leaderboard rank to accuracy-per-dollar at a quality floor, which is where mid-tier and open models can win share.
insights.quote: It is about choosing the model most likely to meet the required quality level at the right cost.
insights.locator: Figure 5 shows that routing is not just about picking the strongest model

themes.theme: No model wins every task group

insights.claim: On Terminal-Bench Hard with the Terminus agent, DeepSeek V4 has the highest overall accuracy yet is not best on every task group — Kimi K2.6 leads on ML and RL tasks and Qwen3.5 397B A17B leads on math and science, with DeepSeek V4 preferred on the remaining six groups.
insights.speaker: Tanay Varshney
insights.so_what: Aggregate benchmark leadership is a poor buying signal; per-domain model strength is the exploitable inefficiency routing monetizes.
insights.quote: While DeepSeek V4 has the highest overall accuracy in this example, it isn’t the best model for every task group.
insights.locator: Consider a system of models performing a computer-use task

insights.claim: Model cost differences in agent workloads come not only from token pricing but from each model's verbosity profile across both tokens and tool calls, so cheap-per-token models are not automatically cheap per task.
insights.speaker: Tanay Varshney
insights.so_what: Total-cost-per-completed-task, not price per million tokens, is the metric to model when forecasting inference spend.
insights.quote: its own verbosity profile, relating not just to tokens but also tool calls
insights.locator: Cost and completion time further complicate the decision

insights.claim: Routing granularity is itself a design variable: the same task-group logic can be applied per individual task or across distinct phases of solving a single task, and a multi-turn agent can be routed once per request or re-routed at every step.
insights.speaker: Tanay Varshney
insights.so_what: Finer routing granularity increases achievable savings but raises deployment complexity — the tradeoff dial to watch as routing products mature.
insights.locator: Importantly, a router must consider not only which signals

insights.claim: Effective routing decisions draw on three distinct signal classes — which models can solve the task (capabilities), the latency and cost of each (cost profile), and system-level signals enabling reliable handoffs (infrastructure).
insights.speaker: Tanay Varshney
insights.so_what: A checklist for evaluating any competing routing product: a router missing the infrastructure class cannot deliver invisible handoffs in production.
insights.locator: Broadly, effective routing decisions rely on signals from three areas

insights.claim: Routing signals can be extracted from three observation points — the request itself via classification or embeddings, the model's internal states via logprobs, residual stream, or attention matrices, and the running system via pricing, latency, load, and agent errors.
insights.speaker: Tanay Varshney
insights.so_what: Access to model internals is a structural advantage for open-weight models over closed APIs in routing, quietly favoring whoever hosts the weights.
insights.quote: A router can examine the model logprobs, cascades, assess agentic trace, model’s residual stream, attention matrices, leverage, etc.

insights.claim: NeMo Switchyard's LLM classifier router uses an LLM as judge to pick a model then maintains session affinity with it, deliberately avoiding repeated reclassification of work that has not materially changed during a task.
insights.speaker: Tanay Varshney
insights.so_what: Affinity is the cheap fix for judge-overhead eating the savings; a design detail to check in any routing vendor's cost math.
insights.locator: The LLM classifier uses an LLM as a judge

insights.claim: The stage router infers required model capability from recent tool activity — severe errors, repeated unproductive work, or prolonged exploration push a turn to the capable model, while steady writes and edits after tests pass favor the efficient model.
insights.speaker: Tanay Varshney
insights.so_what: Behavioral telemetry, not prompt text, is the routing signal that unlocked Cognition's near-frontier-at-lower-cost result; expect it to be copied across coding agents.
insights.quote: Severe errors, repeated unproductive work, or prolonged exploration push the turn toward the capable model.
insights.locator: For each turn, the stage router examines recent tool activity

insights.claim: The escalation router starts every conversation on a lower-cost model and promotes the session to a more capable one only when an LLM judge detects sustained difficulty, converting the classifier approach from a static to an adaptive policy.
insights.speaker: Tanay Varshney
insights.so_what: This is the specific mechanism behind the 74% LangChain cost cut — cheap-by-default with escalation is the pattern to look for in production agent stacks.
insights.locator: Escalation routing starts each conversation with a lower-cost model

insights.claim: The tunable prefill router trains a shared-trunk MLP on an LLM's residual stream to predict each candidate model's likelihood of answering a query correctly, replacing hand-written heuristics with learned per-model accuracy predictions.
insights.speaker: Tanay Varshney
insights.so_what: Learned routers turn accumulated workload traces into a proprietary asset, creating data-network effects for whoever operates the routing layer at scale.
insights.locator: During training, the prefill router extracts the LLM’s residual stream

insights.claim: NeMo Switchyard's switchyard-libsy SDK gives every model target a semantic name that a client maps to a provider endpoint and model ID, so teams can swap models, endpoints, or providers without touching the routing integration.
insights.speaker: Tanay Varshney
insights.so_what: Provider abstraction commoditizes the model underneath and moves switching costs into the routing layer — the layer NVIDIA is giving away free.
insights.quote: This separation keeps the routing logic independent of a specific provider.

insights.claim: The NeMo Switchyard reference server impersonates an LLM gateway by accepting OpenAI, Anthropic, and Responses API request formats and returning the expected response shapes, while logging the selected model, decision rationale, token usage, latency, and outcomes.
insights.speaker: Tanay Varshney
insights.so_what: Drop-in API compatibility means switching costs to try routing are near zero — the fastest path to diverting traffic away from any single provider.
insights.quote: It accepts OpenAI, Anthropic, and Responses API requests, translates them into the internal NeMo Switchyard request format, and returns the expected response format.
insights.locator: The NeMo Switchyard server is a reference

insights.claim: NVIDIA has lined up routing distribution across the entire agent stack at launch — Cognition, Nous Research, Ramp and LangChain on workflows; LiteLLM, Kong, Classmethod and Boomi on infrastructure; Cadence and Siemens on EDA and formal verification.
insights.speaker: Tanay Varshney
insights.so_what: Breadth of day-one partners is the tell that NVIDIA intends Switchyard to become the default routing standard rather than a demo; track adoption in LiteLLM and Kong as the leading indicator.

insights.claim: NVIDIA's benchmark framing pairs its own Nemotron 3.5 Lightning model as the default workhorse against third-party frontier models used only for escalation, implying a strategy in which routing systematically shifts volume toward NVIDIA-aligned open models.
insights.speaker: Tanay Varshney
insights.so_what: The routing layer is not neutral infrastructure — whoever writes the default policy allocates inference demand, and NVIDIA is writing it while shipping the models and the silicon underneath.
insights.locator: routing requests between NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning

insights.claim: NVIDIA concedes that despite shipping the library, building a useful production-ready routing system remains a very difficult engineering challenge, and has open-sourced Switchyard so third parties contribute routing algorithms.
insights.speaker: Tanay Varshney
insights.so_what: Open-sourcing the hard, unsolved layer buys ecosystem R&D and standard-setting without charging for it — the same playbook as CUDA-adjacent tooling.
insights.quote: building a useful and production-ready routing system remains a very difficult engineering challenge
